runs.text: Made by Arshad · 28-fund review
Where each of the 28 funds stands

Nine funds are heavily exposed to an AI-led sell-off, but AI is not the only threat. Oil lurching on every Iran headline (about $94–96 on 12 Nov, down from $115 in late October), a yen at almost 160 per dollar, the level that has triggered intervention, a 10-year US yield back above 5% with a December Fed hike close to certain, and rising tension around Taiwan each hit different funds. Combining all of these, 11 funds rate High or Very high overall risk. Only the money market funds and cash are close to safe in every scenario.
Why these 28:

together they form a comprehensive set covering cash in three currencies, government and corporate bonds, developed and emerging-market shares, real estate, commodities, gold and absolute return, across the US, Europe, the UK, Japan, Asia and the Pacific. Almost any market event shows up somewhere in the list.

Update · Fri 13 Nov 2026, 6 am Manila (covers Thursday 12 Nov in Asia and the US session)
NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang resigns; oil jumps as Trump says the US does not need an Iran deal

NVIDIA co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive on Thursday after reports of two affairs, one with a woman US authorities suspect of spying for China. Finance chief Colette Kress is interim CEO. NVIDIA fell as much as 14% and closed about 4.3% lower. The S&P 500 slipped 0.4% to about 7,592, about 2.9% below its record. Brent rose to about $94–96 after Trump said the US does not need a deal with Iran. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 5.1%, gold fell about 3% to under $3,900, and the yen weakened to almost 160 per dollar. NVIDIA reports results on Tuesday. No fund rating changes.

cells.text: What happened
Funds affected
What it means
NVIDIA's CEO resigned.

Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO, president and board member with immediate effect, after the board met late Wednesday over reports of two extramarital affairs. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and the board will look at internal and external candidates (Euronews). NVIDIA fell as much as 14% at the open and closed about 4.3% lower (Kiplinger); RBC cut its price target from $330 to $230 (SF Standard). CoreWeave fell about 8–10% and Nebius about 17%, while AMD and Broadcom rose about 5–6%. The S&P 500 closed 0.4% lower at about 7,592, the Nasdaq 0.4% lower at 25,366 and the Dow 0.4% lower at 52,297 (Kiplinger). Results are due Tuesday 17 Nov, US time.

A governance shock for the most AI-heavy funds (6, 3, 4, 13, 19), where NVIDIA is a top holding. The market held up better than NVIDIA: money moved into AMD and Broadcom rather than out of AI altogether. Tuesday's results, now without Huang, are the next big test for these funds and for Asian chip exposure (24, 22).
Asia slipped on the NVIDIA news; the yen neared 160.

Taiwan fell about 2.6%, Hong Kong about 1.2–1.3%, Japan's Nikkei 0.7% to 60,798.84 and Korea's KOSPI 0.2% to 5,364.26 after giving up early gains. Shanghai fell 0.6% and Australia was flat (AP). Alibaba fell about 6.7% and Tencent 2.6% in Hong Kong on worries the US may curb Chinese access to offshore data centres with advanced chips (Reuters via Kitco). The dollar was at about 159.8 yen. Europe's STOXX 600 hit its first record since August.

Taiwan's fall hits Asia ex-Japan (24) and emerging markets (22) most, through TSMC. The yen at almost 160 is the level traders see as the trigger for intervention: that is a two-way risk for the yen funds (27, 11). Europe ex-UK (5) is holding up best.
Oil jumped as Trump ruled out needing an Iran deal; gold slid.

Trump said the US does not need an agreement with Iran and that the time for a deal has passed, clouding a reported Qatari plan under which Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz in return for an end to the US blockade (Le Private Banker). Iran's foreign minister said its offer to reopen the strait within two days still stands if the war ends on all fronts. Brent rose to about $94 by midday and about $95.8 late in the day (AP), despite Saudi output reaching its highest since the war began. Gold fell about 2.9% to roughly $3,885 an ounce, near its 30 Oct one-year low, as the dollar firmed (Yahoo Finance).

Higher oil helps the commodity fund (12) and the UK fund (8), with its oil majors, but hurts oil importers in Europe and Asia (5, 22, 23, 27). The gold miners fund (1) is likely to have fallen sharply again: gold is behaving like a risk asset, not a shelter.
Bond yields rose as markets reopened.

The 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 5.10–5.12% from 4.98% on Tuesday, and the 30-year to about 5.44% (Yahoo Finance, AP). San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said further tightening will be needed. CME FedWatch still shows a December quarter-point hike as certain, with about 13% odds of a half point (Reuters via Kitco). Weekly jobless claims rose 9,000 to 200,000, slightly above forecasts, and October home sales were the slowest in more than 16 years (AP).

More pressure on the bond funds (28, 26, 25, 9) and listed real estate (2), which suffer most as yields climb. Friday's producer-price report could add to it. Cash and money market funds (14, 10) keep earning more as rates rise.
Coming up (Manila):

US October producer prices Fri 13 Nov, 9:30 pm; Japan Q3 GDP Mon 16 Nov; NVIDIA results Wed 18 Nov, early morning (Tue 17 Nov, US time); Fed minutes Thu 19 Nov, early morning; Anthropic's market debut expected around 19–20 Nov; US November jobs report Fri 4 Dec, 9:30 pm; Fed decision 8–9 Dec, with a hike fully priced.

NVIDIA's results are now the week's main event for the AI-heavy funds (6, 13). Another hot price report would raise half-point hike odds and hurt the bond funds (28, 26, 25, 9). Weak Japanese GDP would complicate a Bank of Japan hike and weigh on the yen funds (27, 11).

AI-crash scenario
Who gets hurt, who holds

In an AI-led crash I estimate the most AI-concentrated funds could fall 30–40%, broad developed-market equity funds 20–30%, and cash would hold its value. Government bonds would likely gain a few percent, but only if the crash lowers inflation fears rather than arriving with another oil shock.

My estimates from each fund's AI concentration, equity beta and volatility, calibrated to the 2000–02 dot-com bust (S&P 500 about −49%), 2022 (MSCI World −18%, US Treasuries −13%) and Korea's July 2026 chip crash (KOSPI −40% in six weeks). Not forecasts.
Scenario assumed.

AI capital spending is cut sharply, US mega-cap tech falls 40–50%, the S&P 500 falls 25–35% and Asian chip stocks repeat their July 2026 slide. The Fed responds by cutting rates. If inflation stays high instead (for example, the Strait of Hormuz closes again), the bond funds would not rise and only cash would hold.
Liquidity.
Every fund deals daily; settlement is typically 1–3 business days plus any platform processing time. In a crash the practical risks are:
Emerging-market and Asian equity funds (22, 24) and the commodity swap fund (12) can see prices gap and dealing spreads widen.
Funds can apply swing pricing or, in extreme cases, defer large redemptions; this matters most for the active and EM funds.
Selling after a fall locks in the loss. The 2000–02 and 2022 sell-offs both had sharp rebounds that punished late sellers.

Beyond AI
Eight other risks in the news now, and which funds they hit
An AI crash is one way to lose money; these are the others. Several are already moving markets this month. Numbers link to each fund's analysis.

1 · Yen turmoil

The yen fell to about 163 per dollar in late July, prompting a joint US–Japan intervention (Japan reportedly spent around $85bn) that pushed it to 155. By mid-August most of that gain had reversed. Japan had already spent ¥11.7 trillion defending the yen in April–May. It was near 158 on 27 Oct, and Finance Minister Katayama has warned she is ready to act again, with traders watching 160. In the week to 6 Nov the dollar traded between about 157.3 and 158.8 yen; hawkish Bank of Japan minutes and the stock rout helped the yen, but the strong US jobs report pushed the dollar back to the mid-158s. The pressures are a slow Bank of Japan (held at 1.25% on 30 Oct, though it signalled more hikes), PM Takaichi's 19 Oct signal that about ¥10 trillion of tax cuts may be funded with deficit bonds (debt is 204% of GDP), 10-year JGB yields near 3%, and an oil import bill that has only just started to ease (Brent near $98 on 6 Nov, from $115 in late October). On 12 Nov the dollar reached about 159.8 yen, the closest yet to 160. The move can run either way: intervention or a carry-trade unwind could lift the yen 5% in days.

2 · Oil shock and the Strait of Hormuz

Brent settled at $115.32 on 28 Oct, about 75% higher than a year ago. After the 3 Nov US election, Brent fell 8.7% to $94.62 on 4 Nov as markets priced pressure to end the war, and it ended the week of 6 Nov at $98.32, down about 16%, its steepest weekly fall since 2020. On 8 Nov the US launched "Task Force Iron Gate" to curb Iran's trade over land and the Caspian Sea, and on 9 Nov Brent fell about 5% to roughly $93–94, its lowest since 31 Aug. On 10 Nov Brent briefly fell below $90 for the first time since August, ending near $91.8, after Trump said the war was militarily effectively over. On 11 Nov Iran denied talks and said the strait stays shut until its conditions are met; monitors counted at least 37 attacks on ships so far in November, the most of any month in the war. On 12 Nov Trump said the US does not need a deal, clouding a reported Qatari plan to reopen the strait, and Brent rose to about $94–96. Nothing is agreed, and the strait has been largely closed since March. This is a two-way risk. A deal could send oil sharply lower; Brent fell to about $72 during the brief June truce. A longer closure keeps inflation and rates high.

3 · Sticky inflation and rising bond yields

US CPI rose to 3.7% in September (core 2.6%), and markets briefly priced about 50% odds of a second Fed hike this week. The Fed held on 28 Oct in a 10–2 vote, with both dissenters wanting a hike. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.35%, the highest since 2002, and Pimco's CIO has said 6% is possible. On 6 Nov a strong October jobs report (165,000 jobs against about 65,000 expected, unemployment 4.1%) lifted the 2-year yield to 4.51% and the 10-year to 4.86%, and pushed CME odds of a December hike to about 77%. On 9 Nov China's October factory prices rose 5.7% from a year earlier, a four-year high, and CME odds of a December Fed hike were still above 80% even as oil fell. On 10 Nov October CPI rose 0.4% in the month (core 0.3%), above forecasts; the 10-year yield jumped to about 5.01%, a December hike became close to fully priced, and Fed Governor Waller said a half-point move could be considered. On 11 Nov US bond markets were shut for Veterans Day; CME odds still showed a December hike fully priced, with about 13% odds of a half point, and Governor Bowman said there is still work to do on inflation. Rising yields hurt bonds, REITs and expensive growth stocks at the same time, as in 2022, when stocks and bonds fell together.

4 · French debt stress and a weaker euro

France's 10-year yield hit 4.98% on 21 Oct, a 24-year high, and its spread over Germany reached 157 bp, the widest since the euro crisis. EUR/USD fell 3.9% between 9 Sep and 23 Oct even though the ECB raised rates twice this year to 2.50%. Eurozone inflation is 3.8%, and the October PMI fell to a four-month low. On 29 Oct the ECB held, the euro touched a 17-month low, and Lagarde's early exit (7 Feb 2027, before the French election) was confirmed.

China held live-fire drills across five sea areas on 12–17 Oct, coast-guard ships harassed Taiwanese vessels on 18 Oct, and on 16 Oct Beijing drafted export curbs on about 40 technologies, including AI and chips. On 15 Oct foreign investors sold NT$165bn of Taiwan stocks in one day, Korean outflows for October passed $10bn, the Philippine peso passed 63 per dollar for the first time, and India and Indonesia intervened to support their currencies.

6 · AI debt inside "safe" bond funds

AI-related borrowing has passed roughly $466–500bn this year and makes up about 10% of the largest long-term investment-grade bond ETFs. Oracle's 5-year CDS more than doubled to about 308 bp, Meta's and NVIDIA's hit records in October, and CoreWeave's implies a default probability above 60%. Pimco as a firm bought $18bn of Meta's Hyperion data-centre bond. On 28 Oct Alphabet reported that its long-term debt had jumped from $46.5bn to $125.1bn in a year, alongside $12.4bn of stock sales, to pay for AI. On 2 Nov Oracle filed to sell $10bn of stock and $10bn of senior notes for the same purpose. After the 3 Nov election, analysts flagged Democrats' openness to data-centre moratoriums, and on 4 Nov AI-infrastructure names fell (NVIDIA −3.2%, CoreWeave −9.9%, Vistra −13.8%) even as the market rallied. On 5 Nov the chip index fell 12.3% and the Nasdaq entered correction, as investors priced a slower, costlier AI build-out. On 11 Nov CoreWeave said it expects about $9bn of customer prepayments over three months and plans no more expensive debt through 2027; its shares jumped more than 20% and the chip index about 7%.

7 · UK Budget and gilts

The 10-year gilt yield touched 5.53% on 8 Oct, the highest since 2007. UK inflation is 3.5%, and markets expect a Bank of England hike on 5 Nov. The 28 Oct Budget kept about £15bn of fiscal headroom and gilts held steady, but it doubled the bank surcharge to 6%, a cost for the UK fund's banks.

8 · Gold's correction and Australia's rate hikes

Gold briefly fell below $4,000 on 23 Oct, about a quarter under its January record. It dropped alongside stocks as leveraged investors raised cash, so it did not behave as a safe haven that day. It slipped again on 29 Oct and fell 3.3% to a one-year low of $3,899 on 30 Oct as tech sold off, just above Standard Chartered's $3,886 warning level, then rebounded to $3,957 on 2 Nov and $4,070 on 4 Nov. It gained about 4.5% in the week to 6 Nov, its best week since August, ending near $4,050–4,080. On 12 Nov it fell about 2.9% to roughly $3,885 as the dollar firmed on Fed hike bets. In Australia, the RBA has hiked four times this year to 4.60%, CPI is 4.0%, and Q3 core inflation of 3.7% beat forecasts on 28 Oct, and on 3 Nov the RBA hiked a fifth time to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, in a split 6–3 vote that dropped its tightening bias.

November so far. The 3 Nov midterms, in which Democrats won both houses of Congress, set off the sharpest AI sell-off of the year on worries about slower data-centre building. On 5 Nov the chip index fell 12%, its worst day since 2020, and the Nasdaq entered a correction. In the week to 6 Nov the S&P 500 lost 2.7% and the Nasdaq 3.4% (AP); Japan's Nikkei lost 9.3%, leaving it more than 20% below its June record (Yahoo Finance), and Korea's KOSPI 11.7% (Seoul Economic Daily). Brent fell about 16% on hopes of a US–Iran deal (CNBC), while a strong jobs report kept a December Fed hike likely (InvestmentNews). On 9 Nov Wall Street rebounded: the S&P 500 rose 2.3% and the chip index about 7%, while NVIDIA fell 4.4% on a board probe of its CEO and Brent dropped to about $93–94 (Reuters). On 10 Nov hotter October inflation (0.4% in the month) pushed the 10-year yield to about 5.01% and the S&P 500 down about 0.4%, with NVIDIA down 6.3%; Asia had rallied, with the KOSPI up 4% (AP). On 12 Nov NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang resigned; NVIDIA fell as much as 14% before paring losses, the S&P 500 slipped 0.4% to about 7,592, and Brent rose after Trump said no Iran deal is needed (Kiplinger, AP).

In an inflationary environment stocks and bonds can fall together, as in 2022. If an AI crash instead triggers a growth scare and Fed cuts, Treasuries and high-quality bonds should rally. Which of those two worlds arrives decides whether the bond funds protect you; only the cash-like funds are safe in both.
Fund by fund
Holdings, returns, AI exposure and liquidity
Buying in a sell-off
If the S&P 500 falls 5%, 10% or 20%: which funds to add

A guide to which of the 28 funds tend to be worth adding as a sell-off deepens, using the S&P 500's fall from its 7,819 record (6 Oct 2026) as the trigger, because it is the market's main gauge. The idea is to add the steadier, low-AI funds first and the high-growth, AI-heavy funds only once they are much cheaper. Purchases are funded mainly from cash and from bonds that have risen. Where we are now: the S&P 500 closed at about 7,592 on Thu 12 Nov, roughly 2.9% below its record, after NVIDIA's CEO resigned. It is still above the −5% level (~7,430), which is about 2.1% lower. The −10% level (~7,040) is about 7.3% lower.

runs.text: Nobody can pick the bottom. Splitting purchases across the three levels means you are never all-in too early or left with all your cash. The dot-com and 2022 sell-offs both had sharp rallies on the way down.

In an AI or growth crash, Treasuries usually rise, so selling some bonds to buy stocks works. In an oil or inflation shock, bonds may fall too: fund purchases from cash (14) instead, and consider trimming the commodity fund (12), which is likely to have risen.

A general guide based on each fund's AI exposure, volatility and typical behaviour in past sell-offs (2000–02, 2022, Korea's July 2026 chip crash). It is not a forecast and not personal advice. The right amounts depend on each investor's horizon, currency and existing mix.
Fund list
16 providers, 28 funds
Chosen to be comprehensive: between them, these 28 funds cover every major asset class, region and currency, so the list can show how almost any market event plays out.
Data notes & sources
How the figures were put together
Returns

are total returns in the share-class currency, net of fees; 5-year figures are annualised. EUR, GBP and JPY classes are shown in those currencies, not USD. Most are to 30 September 2026; some to 31 August or earlier where that was the latest public figure.
(e) estimates

come from published NAVs (gold miners, Japan, iShares Global Government Bond) or from a sister share class adjusted for currency or hedging cost (Schroder Asian Opportunities, Pimco EUR, Vanguard Global Bond EUR YTD). Treat them as roughly ±2 points.
Proxies:

Europe ex-UK, North America and Pacific use the Institutional class of the same fund; Fulcrum uses its US twin FARIX; NT Climate uses its master fund; GS Quartix uses the R2 USD class. Other share classes of the same funds may differ by 0.05–0.5% a year in fees.
Not publicly available:
the USD cash account rate, L&G Diversified EUR returns, the L&G Diversified USD 1-year return, and Vanguard Japan 1- and 5-year returns. The fund providers can supply them on request.
AI-crash estimates
are my judgement, not model output or forecasts.
Volatility 1–7
(shown as "Risk 1–7" in the earlier version) is my rating on the familiar SRI scale for how much each fund's price swings; it is not the official KID rating.
Other key risks
are non-AI threats backed by news from 4–26 October 2026: currencies, oil, inflation and rates, sovereign debt, geopolitics and credit. Each is rated Low, Medium or High for that fund.
Overall risk

combines AI exposure, those other risks and volatility into one judgement, on a scale from Very low to Very high, for an investor whose spending currency is the US dollar. Funds 11 and 15 carry a note because their risk is much lower in their own currency. These ratings are my judgement and will change with the news; the dates to watch are listed under Other risks.
This page is research to inform your own decision. I am not a licensed financial adviser, and the right mix depends on your horizon, currency and other assets.
